RUBRIC: Pitch & Demonstration. ~10 s. “We’re [team], and this is HAVen: HAV for hand-arm vibration, and a safe haven from it.” Then straight to the team.

RUBRIC: Division bonus (team composition, up to 3 pts). ~15 s. Name each person’s program and what they built, and stress the mix: hardware, firmware, backend and app. That mix is what the Standard Division bonus rewards.

STILL TO ADD: Abduljabbar’s program and year, and Ali’s photo. Check each role matches what that person actually built.

RUBRIC: Impact & Real-World Relevance (10). ~40 s. Make it human first: “Imagine using a jackhammer every day. Years later your fingers go white and numb in the cold, and you can’t button your shirt. That’s hand-arm vibration syndrome, and it’s permanent.” Then the three numbers.

If asked how common it is: it depends heavily on the tool and years of exposure; go to the Impact backup slide (18).

RUBRIC: Creativity & Innovation (10). ~40 s. Hold up the sleeve. “Our sleeve has two sensors. At the wrist, an accelerometer measures the tool’s vibration. Up on the forearm, EMG electrodes read your grip muscles. We only count exposure while the tool is shaking AND gripped, and it fits under the gloves workers already wear.”

If asked “why not a watch?”: the grip muscles are in the forearm, not the wrist.

RUBRIC: Technical Execution (10) + Impact. ~30 s. “So how do we know how much vibration is too much? We don’t invent it. Europe and the UK set two legal lines, measured with the ISO 5349 method: 100 points, the action level, where you must start cutting exposure, and 400 points, the daily limit, where you stop. A jackhammer at a typical 12 m/s² hits the action level in about 21 minutes and the limit in about 83.”

Formula on the slide: A(8) = a × √(T / 8 h), the ISO 5349-1 daily exposure, where a is the vibration magnitude and T the hours of tool use. Points = 100 × (A(8) / 2.5)², which equals 2 × a² × hours. Math if asked: points = 2 × a² × hours. 2 × 12² = 288 points per hour; 100/288 h ≈ 21 min, 400/288 h ≈ 83 min. 12 m/s² is HSE’s typical road-breaker value. 400 isn’t double 100 because harm follows vibration energy (acceleration squared): 5 m/s² is twice 2.5, so four times the points.

RUBRIC: Technical Execution & Problem-Solving (10). ~20 s. “Under the hood: the sleeve is an ESP32 with an EMG front end on the forearm and an accelerometer at the wrist, streaming over Wi-Fi. The phone app does all the math live, with no server. The hard parts were separating real tool vibration from normal arm movement, and a two-step grip calibration so it works on anyone’s arm.”

CHECK with Salaar/Abduljabbar that each line matches what you built (EMG 1 kHz, IMU 500 Hz, Wi-Fi, phone computes everything) and swap in your real hardest problem if it’s different. Judges score technical execution partly on the problems you solved, so name one concretely.

RUBRIC: Prototype Functionality & Usability (10) + Pitch & Demonstration (10). ~2 min. One person demos, one narrates. Turn demo speed on and press “Reset demo” / “Clear today’s points” before you start.

1. Calibrate the wearer (relax, squeeze).
2. Massage gun on: tool use detected, points climb.
3. Point at the time left counting down.
4. Reach 100 points: the action-level alarm fires.
5. Put the gun down: counting stops (it only counts while the tool shakes and is gripped).
6. Open the Overview and flip week → month → year (sample history, labelled).

REHEARSE each step on the real app: drop any step that isn’t working rather than demoing it live. If the hardware fails, play the backup video immediately. Don’t debug live.

RUBRIC: Feasibility & Continuation (10) + Impact. ~20 s. “Today’s dose is only half the story. The app keeps every day, so a worker and their supervisor can see weeks, months and a year at a glance. It shows the ISO standard’s years-to-risk estimate and gives advice from EU and UK guidance, and a supervisor can lower one worker’s daily limit.” The numbers: 31.8 × A(8)^−1.06 (ISO 5349-1 Annex C). At the action level, A(8) = 2.5 m/s²: about 12 years. At the daily limit, A(8) = 5.0 m/s²: about 6 years. The standard’s formula is an older fit, and later research suggests it is conservative. Our A(8) comes from an unweighted wrist sensor, so the input is an estimate too.

Say “group estimate”, never “this worker will get HAVS in X years”. The risk numbers come from ISO 5349 and the EU/UK rules, not our own medical judgement. Historical days in the demo are sample data and are labelled that way in the app.

RUBRIC: Feasibility & Continuation (10). ~10 s. Land the takeaway, say the one-line next step, and stop talking. Stay on this slide during Q&A until a question matches a backup slide (index on slide 10).
Presenter-only cheat sheet. In Present mode type a slide number and press Enter to jump to it. Practise jumping to 11, 13 and 15: competition, cost and who buys are the most likely questions.

Q: “Who else does this?” Answer: “Glad you asked. This is a proven market: Reactec alone serves tens of thousands of workers and grew revenue about 41% in 2023. Today’s products are watches, tool tags and professional meters that measure the tool. We measure the worker, with a sleeve that fits under any glove, at about C$19 in parts.”

Don’t quote market share %; no public data exists. If a judge names another product, acknowledge it and go to the edge slide (12).

Q: “What makes you different?” Answer: walk the four boxes in ~20 seconds: the sleeve under any glove (practical), muscle effort and fatigue (technical), the long-term view (prevention), built for Canada (market).

Don’t claim nobody else senses grip; say we read grip MUSCLE effort and fatigue from the forearm, in a sleeve.

Q: “How much does it cost?” Answer: “At 100 units, one HAVen sleeve costs about C$18.69 to make: the ESP32 module, accelerometer, EMG board, a factory-assembled PCB with power and charging, and a compression sleeve. Competitor devices start around £1,150 for a watch system and go past £2,000 for a professional meter.”

That’s parts and assembly, not retail price or software; say so if asked. FILL IN what the * on the MPU-6050 line means (e.g. price assumption or substitute part), or delete the asterisk.

Q: “What would the real product look like?” / “Would workers actually wear this?” Answer: point at the renders and walk the four upgrades: the wrist pod (sealed electronics, rigid wrist mount), the two electrodes built into the sleeve, the washable sleeve itself. Be clear the prototype uses dev boards and gel electrodes; the production design removes setup. These are concept renders of the design, not CAD or a built part: say so if asked. WHY BACKUP: a budget prototype can make judges doubt feasibility. This slide answers that only when asked, without spending pitch time on a product that doesn’t exist yet.

Q: “Who would buy this?” / “Why would a company pay for something that might show they’re over the limit?” Answer: “Our advisor raised exactly that, so we looked beyond employers. Unions and workers want their own exposure record, because HAVS compensation claims are hard to prove in Canada. Rental companies can rent it with the tool; Speedy Hire in the UK already did this with HAV meters. And employers have a financial reason: Alberta’s WCB gives COR-certified companies a 10% premium refund in year one and 5% after, so a better safety program pays for itself.” CAUTION: the WCB refund is for COR certification overall, not for buying this device; say “supports their safety program”, not “gets them a rebate”. The union/worker angle is a hypothesis to validate with real union reps. WHY BACKUP: the “who pays” question comes up in almost every Q&A, and your advisor specifically flagged it.

Q: “How big is the market?” Answer: “We’d start with Alberta construction, about 266,000 workers, and sell through contractors, unions and rental firms. The UK shows the demand is real: one company alone had about 70,000 workers on its wearable. After construction: mining, oil and gas, manufacturing, forestry, rail.” DON’T invent a total market size in dollars. If you want one, compute it live and say it’s an assumption: e.g. 10% of Alberta construction workers × your monthly price × 12. WHY BACKUP: a beachhead + proof + expansion story answers “is this a business?” in 20 seconds without made-up market-size numbers.

Q: “What’s next?” / “What would you do with the prize?” Answer: walk left to right in ~20 seconds, then name what the prize money funds. Validation comes first because accuracy is your biggest open question. FILL IN: the bottom line with concrete uses of the seed funding and in-kind services (e.g. a reference vibration meter rental, a production PCB run, a pilot with one contractor). WHY BACKUP: Feasibility & Continuation is 10 points, and the prize is development funding. If a judge doesn’t ask, consider pulling one sentence of this into the thank-you.

Q: “What impact would this have?” / “Does this matter to companies?”
Answer: “Where exposure is regulated and measured, cases fall: new UK HAVS benefit cases dropped from about 1,200 in 2010 to about 220 in 2024. Where it isn’t managed, the bill comes later: around 145,000 vibration white finger claims were settled for former British Coal miners. And in Canada few claims are accepted, partly because workers have no exposure record; HAVen gives them one.”

CAREFUL: the UK drop is correlation (regulation, monitoring and fewer exposed jobs all play a part). The coal schemes’ total cost (about £4.1bn compensation plus £2.3bn admin) covers vibration AND lung disease, so only quote the 145,000 VWF claims as vibration-specific.
